Paver sealing and re-sanding in Melbourne

Seal the paver, lock the joint

Most paving problems are joint problems. Sand washes out, water sits in the gap, moss takes it, weeds root in the silt that replaces the sand, and eventually the pavers stop interlocking and start rocking. Re-sanding fixes it. Sealing is what stops it happening again.

  • Kiln dried or polymeric, your choice
  • Sealer binds the joint as well as the paver
  • Weeds lose the silt they root in
Get A Quote 0400 638 010

Two steps, in this order

Re-sand, then seal. Sealing a paved area with empty joints protects the pavers and leaves the actual problem in place, and filling joints after sealing means the sand has nothing binding it.

The cleaning and ordinary joint refill are covered under paving and patio cleaning, which is where most jobs start. This page is the next decision: whether to use a polymeric sand instead of ordinary kiln dried, and whether to put a sealer over the top. Both cost more, both last considerably longer, and on a patio you actually use they are usually the right call.

Which sand

The decision that does most of the work

Both are swept into the joint and compacted. What happens next is what differs.
  Kiln dried sand Polymeric sand
What it is Clean, dry, graded silica sand Graded sand with a binder through it, activated with water
After it is in Stays loose in the joint Sets semi-hard, like a flexible grout
Washing out Will wash out again over a few years Stays put through rain and hosing
Weeds Blocks them while the joint stays full Blocks them for considerably longer
Ants They can excavate it They mostly cannot
Flexibility Fully flexible. Pavers can still settle and adjust Semi flexible. It can crack if the base moves significantly
Cost Lower, and included in a standard paving clean Higher, quoted separately
Best for Most domestic patios, especially with a sealer over it Driveways, high traffic areas and anywhere you are tired of re-sanding

Swipe for the rest of the columns

What the sealer adds

Beyond protecting the paver itself

It binds the top of the joint

A joint stabilising sealer soaks into the surface of the sand and glues the top few millimetres together. That is the layer that washes out first, so stabilising it is most of the benefit.

The pavers stop absorbing

Concrete and clay pavers are porous. Sealed, barbecue fat, red wine, leaf tannin and oil sit on the surface and wipe off instead of staining.

Colour comes back

A topical sealer deepens paver colour the way rain does. On a tired patio that is often a bigger visual change than the cleaning was.

Growth has nowhere to start

Moss colonises the damp joint first. A bound, sealed joint holds far less water and gives it nothing to root into.

Sealing will not fix a base problem

If pavers have dropped, lifted or gone out of level, the bedding or the base underneath has moved and no amount of sand or sealer corrects that. It is a relaying job. We will tell you if that is what we can see rather than sealing over it and leaving you to discover it.

Questions

Asked about joints and sealing

Do I need to re-sand before sealing?

Yes, always. Sealing a paved area with empty joints protects the pavers and leaves the actual problem exactly where it was. The joint is what stops pavers moving and stops weeds rooting, so filling it comes first.

Is polymeric sand worth the extra?

On a driveway or a high traffic area, generally yes, because ordinary sand washes out faster where it is driven on and hosed down. On a domestic patio, kiln dried sand with a stabilising sealer over it usually gets you most of the benefit for less.

The case against polymeric is flexibility: it sets semi-hard, so if the base moves it can crack. On a well laid patio that is not a concern.

Will sealing change how the pavers look?

A topical sealer deepens the colour, which on tired concrete pavers is usually a bigger visual change than the cleaning. If you want no change at all, a penetrating sealer protects without altering the appearance, but it does less for the joint.

We can do a test area so you can see it dry before committing the whole patio.

How long before I can walk on it?

Polymeric sand needs to be wetted and then left, usually overnight. Sealer is touch dry in a few hours and walkable the next day. Furniture back after two or three days, so nothing leaves a mark in a coating that has not fully cured.

How often will it need doing again?

Three to five years for a sealed patio, against roughly every two for an unsealed one that has to be cleaned and re-sanded. Polymeric sand under a sealer is the longest lasting combination.

Can you seal bluestone and travertine paving?

Yes, and both benefit more than concrete pavers do because they are considerably more porous. Bluestone in particular picks up oil and tannin stains quickly when it is left bare.

Travertine and limestone need a sealer chosen for calcium based stone, and they must never be acid cleaned at any stage, which changes how the preparation is done. Stone and bluestone sealing.
